Newly hatched goslings of the Emperor goose (Anser canagicus) emerge from eggs incubated at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], with hatching occurring after approximately 24.5 days [ab = approximately 24.5 days]. The chicks weigh roughly 81.8 grams [Wwb = roughly 81.8 grams] at the moment of emergence, a modest initial mass that reflects the substantial yolk reserves consumed during development. In contrast, the initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg, representing the total organic investment at the start of incubation, is around 120 grams [Ww0 = around 120 grams]. This substantial egg mass is consistent with the energetic demands of producing a semi-precocial chick capable of rapid locomotion soon after hatching. Field observations from the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta indicate that incubation temperatures are tightly regulated by the attending adult, despite the variable thermal conditions of the Arctic spring.

Once hatched, the downy chicks are led to feeding areas by their parents, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth. A key developmental milestone, the fledging stage, is achieved at 55 days after hatching [tx = 55 days after hatching] under the standard metabolic conditions maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a point marked by full flight feather maturation. This duration, falling within the reported range of 50 to 60 days for development, represents a critical transition as the young birds gain independence from parental care. During this nestling period, the goslings shift from a diet of protein-rich invertebrates to foraging on graminoids and algae, a dietary transition that fuels their high growth rates.

Sexual maturation in the Emperor goose is a protracted process relative to many other waterfowl species. This delay is likely an adaptation to the short Arctic growing season, allowing young birds to accumulate sufficient body reserves before committing to the high energetic costs of reproduction. The ultimate wet weight for adult males, representing their maximum recorded body mass, is 2812 grams [Wwi = 2812 grams], while females attain a slightly lower asymptotic mass of 2766 grams [Wwi = 2766 grams]. This modest sexual size dimorphism, consistent with strong pair bonds and biparental care, places the species among the more size-monomorphic members of the tribe Anserini.

The timing of first reproduction is a key life-history parameter for this long-lived species. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active season at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the time since birth at first brood is approximately 730 days [tR = approximately 730 days], a delay that reflects the need for multiple seasons of resource acquisition before breeding. Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained from captive adult Emperor geese at this same body temperature reveal a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 1612.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 1612.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively high metabolic rate, when scaled to body mass, is consistent with the energetic demands of an endotherm inhabiting a cold, high-latitude environment. The maximum reproductive rate is correspondingly constrained: females typically produce one clutch per breeding season. Clutch size ranges from 3 to 12 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 12 eggs per clutch], and with only one clutch laid each year [F_R_i = one clutch laid each year], the annual fecundity is modest compared to more southerly nesting goose species.

The maximum recorded longevity for the Emperor goose, based on wild banding recaptures, is approximately 25.5 years [am = approximately 25.5 years] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This extended lifespan, among the longest documented for any Arctic-nesting goose, reflects a slow life-history pace characterized by delayed maturity, low annual fecundity, and high adult survival. Such a strategy is common among large-bodied waterfowl that face unpredictable breeding conditions, where the ability to defer reproduction in poor years and survive to breed in multiple seasons is heavily favored. The constraints imposed by a short Arctic summer and high metabolic costs are clearly reflected in the species' overall energetic budget. The interplay between their substantial maintenance requirements and their limited window for successful reproduction underscores the delicate balance that defines the life history of this Alaskan endemic. Future studies comparing these physiological parameters to those of the closely related cackling goose could further illuminate the evolutionary trade-offs shaped by the extreme high-latitude environment.
